title: Single Responsibility Principle
summary: One reason to change, not one method — and the concrete test that tells you when a class has taken on a second job.

slides.markdown:
The **Single Responsibility Principle** (SRP) says a class should have **one reason to change** — not one method, not one line of code. A class that owns both "how we calculate a bill" and "how we format a receipt" has two reasons to change, and a change to one risks breaking the other.

Think of it like a restaurant job: the cook cooks, the cashier charges, the printer prints the receipt. Cram all three into one person and every menu change, price change, and printer change lands on the same overworked employee.

slides.sectionTitle: SRP defined: one reason to change, not "one method"
slides.markdown:
SRP is one of the most misquoted principles in software: people read it as "a class should do one thing" and start splitting every multi-method class apart. The actual definition, from Robert Martin, is narrower: **a class should have only one reason to change** — one axis of business or technical concern that can force an edit.

A class can have five methods and still satisfy SRP, as long as all five exist to serve the same responsibility. `OrderValidator` can have `checkStock()`, `checkAddress()`, and `checkPayment()` and still be single-responsibility, because all three change for the same reason: the rules of "is this order valid" changing.

The unit of analysis is **reasons to change**, not method count.

slides.sectionTitle: The "reason to change" test — how to actually apply it
slides.markdown:
To test a class for SRP, ask: **"who asks for this class to change, and why?"** List every distinct stakeholder or requirement that could trigger an edit. If the list has more than one independent entry, the class is carrying more than one responsibility.

For an `InvoiceService` that computes totals, saves to a database, and emails a PDF: the finance team changes tax rules (recompute), the DBA changes the schema (persistence), and marketing changes the email template (formatting). Three unrelated stakeholders, three reasons to change — that's the signal to split.

A quick heuristic: if you'd hand two of a class's methods to two different teams to own, it's already two responsibilities wearing one name.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a God Class doing 3 jobs vs split into 3 classes
slides.markdown:
![One InvoiceService touched by Finance, DBA, and Marketing versus three separate classes each owned by one stakeholder](assets/srp-split.svg)

The left side is a **God Class**: one file that three unrelated teams all have to touch, so it changes for three unrelated reasons and gets fragile fast. The right side gives each stakeholder exactly one class to own — this is what a violation of common design anti-patterns looks like next to its SRP-compliant fix.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a class mixing persistence + business logic + formatting, then split
Compare: SRP at class level vs method level vs module level
slides.markdown:
SRP is usually taught at the class level, but the same "one reason to change" test applies at every granularity:

| Level | What "one responsibility" means | Violation smell |
|---|---|---|
| Method | Does one logical step, at one level of abstraction | A method that validates, computes, *and* logs |
| Class | Serves one stakeholder/concern; its methods all change together | Methods split cleanly into two unrelated call groups |
| Module/package | Groups classes that change for the same business reason | Two features' code interleaved in the same package |

**How to decide the level:** apply the reason-to-change test wherever you're about to make a cut — a bloated method usually gets fixed by extracting a helper, a bloated class by splitting into collaborators, a bloated module by re-drawing package boundaries.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: over-splitting into many trivial classes ("SRP-itis")
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "SRP means every method should be its own class, so more splitting is always safer."

**Why it's wrong:** splitting past the point where responsibilities are actually distinct creates a maze of tiny classes that all change together anyway — you haven't reduced reasons to change, you've just scattered one reason across five files, making every edit a multi-file hunt.

**Correct model:** stop splitting once each resulting class maps to exactly one real stakeholder or concern. If two "classes" always get edited in the same commit for the same reason, they were never separate responsibilities — merge them back.

slides.sectionTitle: How SRP interacts with cohesion — high cohesion means few reasons to change
slides.markdown:
SRP and **cohesion** are the same idea seen from two angles. Cohesion asks "how tightly do this class's members belong together?"; SRP asks "how many reasons does this class have to change?" A highly cohesive class — where every field and method serves one purpose — almost automatically has one reason to change, because there's only one purpose for anything to change *for*.

When a class feels SRP-compliant on paper but keeps needing multi-part edits, check its cohesion: unrelated fields sharing a class is often the real culprit, not a missing split.

See [Coupling and Cohesion](coupling-and-cohesion) for the full breakdown of cohesion types.

slides.sectionTitle: Interview framing: "tell me about a class you refactored for SRP"
slides.markdown:
This question checks whether you can spot a real violation, not just recite the definition. A strong answer names a concrete class, states the two-plus reasons it changed, and describes the split — not "I made it cleaner."

Example shape: "Our `UserController` handled request parsing, business validation, and response serialization. Product changes to validation and API-contract changes to serialization kept landing in the same file and colliding in code review. I split it into a `UserValidator` and a `UserResponseMapper`, and the controller became a thin coordinator."

Naming the *stakeholders* who each triggered a change is what separates a real story from a rehearsed one.
